title: Brenner's Parade
notebook: Army Day in six days. Brenner wants four divisions, armor support and a flyover down Marshal's Avenue.
Brenner calls it institutional morale. Under Halvek, parades were a show of force.

narrative.text: General Oskar Brenner does not request meetings; he schedules them. When his aide arrived with the briefing folder, it was already assumed you would make time. Halvek allowed the military its pride, and Brenner expects the same from you.

Chancellor. Army Day is in six days. The General Staff has prepared the traditional route down Marshal's Avenue. Four divisions, armor support, flyover by the Air Wing. It is a matter of institutional morale. The soldiers need to know the Palace still values them.

Four divisions and tanks in the capital. Under Halvek, this was a show of force directed at the populace—a reminder of who held the guns. Brenner calls it morale. I call it a warning. He is testing whether I will accept the military as a political actor in my first hundred days.

choices.text: Approve the parade. Tradition is tradition, and the military needs to know I am not their enemy.
Modify it. A parade, yes, but dismounted. No tanks in the capital. Honor the soldiers, not the hardware.
Refuse it. The Republic does not parade its weapons through its own capital. We are a civilian government now.

narrative.text: A wise decision, Chancellor. The men will be gratified. I will ensure the route is secured and the optics are... appropriate for a new government.
Brenner leaves the office looking satisfied. Vyktor, who has been standing by the window, waits until the door is closed before speaking.
The optics will be exactly what Brenner wants them to be. You have just told the General Staff that the Palace will blink first when it comes to the military.
I bought their loyalty with a parade. But loyalty bought with tanks is just a ceasefire waiting to expire. Brenner knows it. And now, so do I.

choices.text: It's done. Let's hope the tanks stay on the avenue.

narrative.text: Dismounted. I see. The soldiers will march, but without their steel. Very well, Chancellor. I will convey your... preference to the General Staff.
He salutes stiffly and departs. It is a compromise, but it is one that leaves both sides slightly unsatisfied. The perfect political outcome.
Brenner reads this as weakness cloaked in compromise. The reformists see it as a half-measure. But the tanks stay in their garages, and for today, that is the only victory that matters.

choices.text: A compromise is a victory neither side can claim. Good.

narrative.text: No parade. Understood. I will inform the garrison that the new Chancellor finds their traditions... distasteful.
He does not salute. He turns and walks out, letting the door close heavily behind him. The silence in the office is thick.
You have just made an enemy of the most powerful man in the military, Katerin. He will not forget this. And neither will his generals.

I drew a line today. No tanks in the capital. No military spectacles. But Vyktor is right—Brenner will remember this. When the time comes that I need the army's loyalty, I may find that I traded it for a principle.

choices.text: Principles are all I have right now, Vyktor. Let him be angry.
